text: Which of the following functions grows the fastest asymptotically?
expl:
Order by class: log log n, 3n + 7, n!, nⁿ.

Concept: Standard growth ladder: 1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ. Polynomials lose to exponentials, exponentials to factorials.

Method: Take logs of both functions: the one with the larger logarithm grows faster (log nⁿ = n log n vs log 2ⁿ = n). Compare exponents when the bases match.

Watch out: n^(log n) is faster than any polynomial but slower than 2ⁿ; (log n)^k is slower than n^ε for every ε > 0.

expl:
Here a = 3, b = 2, so n^(log_b a) = n^(log_2 3) = n^1.585, while f(n) = Θ(n^2). Comparing the two: f(n) is larger ⇒ the root dominates: Θ(f(n)).

Concept: For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) compare f(n) with n^(log_b a): smaller by a polynomial factor → Θ(n^(log_b a)); equal → Θ(n^(log_b a) log n); larger (and regular) → Θ(f(n)).

Method: Compute log_b a, compare it with the exponent of f(n), then read off the case. For f(n) = n^k log^p n with k equal to log_b a the answer is n^k log^(p+1) n.

Watch out: The theorem does not apply when f(n) is not polynomially comparable (e.g. n/log n) or a is not constant.

Classic DP over capacity gives 75.

Concept: 0/1 knapsack picks each item whole or not at all: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i−1][w], v_i + dp[i−1][w − w_i]) when w_i ≤ w.

Method: Fill the table row by row for items and capacities, then read dp[n][W]; to recover the items walk back from dp[n][W] checking where the value changed.

Watch out: Greedy by value/weight ratio is only optimal for the fractional version; O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial.
subject: ALGO

text: Matrices A1..A4 have dimensions 4 × 12 × 4 × 20 × 6 (Ai is d[i−1] × d[i]). Minimum number of scalar multiplications to compute A1·A2·…·A4?
expl:
Matrix-chain DP gives 768.

Concept: Matrix-chain multiplication chooses the parenthesisation with the fewest scalar products; m[i][j] = min over k of m[i][k] + m[k+1][j] + p_{i−1}·p_k·p_j.

Method: Compute chains of increasing length; multiplying a p×q matrix by a q×r matrix costs p·q·r scalar multiplications.

Watch out: The dimension array has n+1 entries for n matrices; the result is only the minimum cost, not the product.

Sum of 2^⌈log₂(h + 2)⌉.

Concept: CIDR describes a network by address and prefix length; the block size is 2^(32 − prefix) addresses, of which two are reserved (network and broadcast). VLSM allocates different prefix lengths per subnet.

Method: Convert requirements to host counts, round up to a power of two (hosts + 2), assign largest subnets first and keep blocks aligned.

Watch out: Usable hosts = 2^h − 2; blocks must start at multiples of their size.

expl:
3 entities + 0 M:N + 2 multivalued = 5.

Concept: Map entities to tables with their keys, M:N relationships to tables with both keys, and 1:N relationships by adding the foreign key to the N side; weak entities include the owner's key.

Method: Count entity tables plus separate relationship tables (only where needed) to get the number of relations.

Watch out: Merge a 1:1 or 1:N relationship into an existing table to reduce the count.

Yes, but only if all transactions commit
expl:
Precedence graph edges: [('T1', 'T2'), ('T2', 'T1')] (has a cycle).

Concept: A schedule is conflict-serializable iff its precedence graph is acyclic; edges Tᵢ → Tⱼ come from conflicting operations (R-W, W-R, W-W on the same item) of different transactions with Tᵢ first.

Method: List the conflicting pairs, draw the graph and test for cycles; an acyclic graph's topological order is an equivalent serial schedule.

Concept: There are 2^(2ⁿ) Boolean functions of n variables; a function is determined by its truth table.

Method: Count truth-table rows (2ⁿ) and raise 2 to that power.

Watch out: Self-dual and monotone function counts need additional constraints.

text: f(x) = 4x + 2 for x < 1 and f(x) = kx² for x ≥ 1. For which value of k is f continuous at x = 1?
expl:
Match left and right limits at x = 1: 6 = k·1.

Concept: A function is continuous at a if lim x→a f(x) exists, f(a) is defined and the two are equal. Removable, jump and infinite discontinuities differ.

Method: Compare left and right limits with f(a); polynomials, exp, sin are continuous everywhere, rational functions except at zero denominators.

Watch out: Continuity does not imply differentiability (|x| at 0).

(a/(a+b))·((a−1)/(a+b−1)).

Concept: For equally likely outcomes P(E) = favourable / total; for n coin tosses there are 2ⁿ outcomes, for two dice 36; use symmetry and complements.

Method: List or count outcomes systematically (tables for dice sums) and divide.

Watch out: Distinguish ordered from unordered outcomes.
subject: ENGM

text: P(A) = 0.02, P(B|A) = 0.95, P(B|¬A) = 0.1. Find P(B). (up to 4 decimals)
expl:
Total probability.

Concept: Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B); total probability P(B) = ΣP(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ); Bayes' rule P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).

Method: Draw a tree or table of the partitioned events, compute P(B) by total probability, then divide.

Watch out: P(A|B) and P(B|A) are different; base rates matter.

```c
fork();
```
expl:

Method: Track which processes execute each fork() (parent returns non-zero, child returns 0) and count the processes created.

Watch out: In A && fork() the fork only runs when A is true; in A || fork() only when A is false.

text: Round-robin time quantum is 4 ms and each context switch costs 0.5 ms. CPU efficiency in percent for CPU-bound processes? (up to 2 decimals)
expl:
q/(q + s).

Concept: Process creation and context switches cost more than thread switches because threads share an address space; user-level threads switch without the kernel but block together.

Method: Compare the overhead components (save/restore registers, TLB flush, kernel entry) for the mechanisms.

Watch out: Kernel threads can run on several CPUs; user-level threads cannot.

text: A 40-bit virtual address uses pages of 2^12 bytes; each page-table entry is 4 bytes and every page-table level must fit exactly in one page. Minimum number of page-table levels required?
expl:
Index bits per level = 12 − log2(4) = 10. Bits to translate = 40 − 12 = 28 → ⌈28/10⌉ = 3.

Concept: A multi-level page table splits the page number into indices per level, each level fitting in one page; the number of levels L and entries per page determine the address split.

Method: Compute entries per page (page size / entry size), bits per level, then levels = ⌈page-number bits / bits per level⌉.

Watch out: Each extra level adds one memory access on a TLB miss.

Index bits per level = 14 − log2(4) = 12. Bits to translate = 44 − 14 = 30 → ⌈30/12⌉ = 3.

Concept: A multi-level page table splits the page number into indices per level, each level fitting in one page; the number of levels L and entries per page determine the address split.

Method: Compute entries per page (page size / entry size), bits per level, then levels = ⌈page-number bits / bits per level⌉.

Watch out: Each extra level adds one memory access on a TLB miss.

text: In a single-level paging system the TLB lookup takes 20 ns and a memory access takes 200 ns. With TLB hit ratio 0.90, the effective memory access time (ns) is
expl:
EAT = h(t+m) + (1−h)(t+2m) = 240.00 ns.

Concept: EAT with a TLB = h·(t_tlb + t_mem) + (1−h)·(t_tlb + 2·t_mem) for a one-level page table; hit ratio h is the key parameter.

Method: Weight the hit and miss paths by their probabilities and add memory accesses (page-table walk + data).

Watch out: On a miss multi-level tables add one access per level.

text: Memory access time is 200 ns and servicing a page fault takes 10 ms. If the page-fault rate is 1 in 1000 accesses, the effective access time in ns is? (up to 1 decimal)
expl:
EAT = (1−p)m + p·S = 10199.8 ns.

Concept: Demand paging loads pages on first use; effective access time EAT = (1−p)·memory time + p·(fault service time), with fault rate p.

Method: Plug p and the access times into EAT; solve for p if EAT is bounded.

Watch out: Fault service time is millions of nanoseconds, so p must be tiny.

text:
What does f(18) return?
```c
int f(int n) { if (n == 1) return 0; return 1 + f(n % 2 ? 3 * n + 1 : n / 2); }
```
expl:
Collatz steps.

Each call adds 1 and moves to 3n+1 (odd n) or n/2 (even n) until n = 1 returns 0.
Chain: 18 → 9 → 28 → 14 → 7 → 22 → 11 → 34 → 17 → 52 → 26 → 13 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1
There are 20 moves before the base case, so f returns 20.

Concept: Evaluate recursive functions by expanding the definition to the base case; many have closed forms (Collatz steps, Fibonacci, GCD by Euclid).

Method: Compute small cases by hand and look for the pattern.

Watch out: Check the base case and whether the recursion reduces its argument.
subject: PDS

text: A singly linked list initially holds [21, 23, 16, 2, 26, 7] (head first). Operations applied in order: insert 32 at the head; insert 54 at the head; insert 48 at the head; delete the head. What is the value of the node at position 1 (0 = head) in the final list?
expl:
Final list: [54, 32, 21, 23, 16, 2, 26, 7].

List after each operation (head first):
insert 32 at the head -> [32, 21, 23, 16, 2, 26, 7]
insert 54 at the head -> [54, 32, 21, 23, 16, 2, 26, 7]
insert 48 at the head -> [48, 54, 32, 21, 23, 16, 2, 26, 7]
delete the head -> [54, 32, 21, 23, 16, 2, 26, 7]

Concept: Linked-list operations rewire next pointers: insertion/deletion at a known node is O(1) but searching is O(n); reversing needs three pointers (prev, curr, next).

Method: Draw the list and apply the pointer updates in order.

Watch out: Update pointers in the right order or the rest of the list is lost.

text: Keys 49 24 46 33 22 56 are inserted in this order into an initially empty BST. Height of the tree (edges on the longest root-to-leaf path)?
expl:
Build the BST: height 3.

Build the tree one key at a time (smaller goes left, larger goes right):
insert 49: the tree is empty, so it becomes the root
insert 24: compare along 49, then place it as the left child of 49
insert 46: compare along 49 → 24, then place it as the right child of 24
insert 33: compare along 49 → 24 → 46, then place it as the left child of 46
insert 22: compare along 49 → 24, then place it as the left child of 24
insert 56: compare along 49, then place it as the right child of 49
Preorder of the final tree: [49, 24, 22, 46, 33, 56]; height = 3 edges.

Concept: A binary search tree keeps left < node < right; inorder traversal gives sorted order; search/insert are O(h), worst case O(n) for sorted insertions.

Method: Insert keys in the given order and read the shape or traversal.

Watch out: The shape depends on insertion order; the number of distinct BSTs on n keys is the Catalan number.

expl:
Simulate AVL insertions.

Concept: An AVL tree keeps balance factor |h_left − h_right| ≤ 1 through rotations (LL, RR, LR, RL); minimum nodes N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1.

Method: Insert in order, check balance factors along the path, and rotate at the first unbalanced node from the inserted leaf.

Watch out: Deletion can need rotations all the way up.

text: Keys 45 33 24 5 28 48 are inserted into an empty min-heap using sift-up. What is the value stored in the last position of the array?
expl:
Final array: [5, 24, 33, 45, 28, 48].

Heap array after each insertion (parent of index i is (i-1)//2, 0-based):
insert 45 at the end, no swap needed -> [45]
insert 33 at the end, sift up (45↔33) -> [33, 45]
insert 24 at the end, sift up (33↔24) -> [24, 45, 33]
insert 5 at the end, sift up (45↔5, 24↔5) -> [5, 24, 33, 45]
insert 28 at the end, no swap needed -> [5, 24, 33, 45, 28]
insert 48 at the end, no swap needed -> [5, 24, 33, 45, 28, 48]

Concept: A binary heap is a complete tree in an array; insert and delete cost O(log n); buildheap is O(n); heap sort is O(n log n) and in place.

Method: Apply sift-up/down operations explicitly to the array.

Watch out: The heap array is not sorted; only parent–child order is guaranteed.

text: In a 3-ary heap stored in a 0-indexed array, what is the index of the parent of the element at index 37?
expl:

Classify each language with the pumping lemma / known machines.

Concept: Classify a language by the machine that recognises it: finite memory → regular; one stack → context-free; bounded tape → context-sensitive; unbounded tape → RE. Use pumping lemmas to show a language is not regular/CF.

Method: Check whether a finite automaton can track the required counts; if comparison of unbounded counts is needed it is not regular.

Watch out: aⁿbⁿ is context-free but not regular; aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not context-free.

text: The class of recursively enumerable languages is closed under which of the following operations? (select all)
expl:
Standard closure table for the Chomsky hierarchy.

Concept: Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation, star, reversal and homomorphism; CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, star and reversal but not intersection or complement; decidable languages are closed under complement, RE languages are not.

Method: Look up the language class and operation in the closure table; if absent, build a counterexample (e.g. aⁿbⁿcᵐ ∩ aᵐbⁿcⁿ).
